_about: Hand-written plain-English renderings of the abstract, one per article, keyed by DOI. These were drafted with an AI assistant and checked by hand; they are summaries, not the authors' words, and not machine-generated from the abstract text at build time. Where a publisher deposited no abstract there is nothing to translate, so the article appears on the dashboard without one.
10.1093/analys/anag031: What is it, exactly, to be taken in by a lie? The authors say deception happens when you stop asking and settle on a wrong answer. That explains why sceptical people are harder to fool, and it comes with practical advice: keep inquiring, don't settle.
10.1093/analys/anag006: Augustine said he knew what time was until somebody asked him. Markosian works through the leading answers - that time is a fourth dimension of spacetime, that it doesn't exist, that it's a logical construction - rejects all of them, and lands on time as a many-sided dimension of reality, more like the moral or the possible than like a spatial axis.
10.1093/analys/anag013: If God has no parts, does it follow that the universe had to exist exactly as it does? That's the 'modal collapse' worry about divine simplicity. The paper examines the latest repair to one such argument, shows the test it depends on is faulty, offers a better test, and concludes the whole family of arguments is in trouble.
10.1093/analys/anae060: You're offered two envelopes, told one holds twice the other, and reasoning seems to say you should always switch - forever. The author argues the puzzle dissolves once you allow your beliefs to be imprecise rather than pinned to exact numbers, which also vindicates the common-sense view that the two envelopes should look equally good to start with.
10.1093/analys/anae089: Can you have a right held against a particular person that everybody has simply by being human? Sreenivasan says no, pointing out that some people are stateless and some children have no living parents. This reply argues that the demand for no exceptions is too strict, and that conditional rights - against your state, or if you have none, against wherever you live - do the job.
10.1093/analys/anaf001: Some philosophers hold there is no fact about what our words refer to, so 'London' might just as well pick out a volcano. Critics say this refutes itself: stating it requires the very determinate reference it denies. The paper works through several versions of that objection and argues each one misdescribes what the position actually claims.
10.1093/arisoc/aoag025: Philosophy now works like a science - thousands of specialists on ever-narrower questions - yet philosophers famously refuse to take each other's conclusions on trust, and disagreement keeps growing. Is the whole enterprise absurd? The author suggests progress is real but happens inside small research communities rather than the field at large, which makes the division of labour defensible after all.
10.1093/arisoc/aoag008: How do you know other people have minds? Nathalie Duddington, a neglected early-twentieth-century philosopher, gave two answers: we perceive minds directly in living bodies, and we are changed by other people in the course of knowing them. The paper develops both, arguing the second gives us something perception alone cannot - a real answer to the solipsist.
10.1093/arisoc/aoaf015: Standing in front of a great painting you feel it means something profound and cannot say what. The author proposes that some artistic meaning is not encoded in the work at all: it is whatever your attention lands on when the artwork is used as a pointing device, and you engage with it well.
10.1093/arisoc/aoag022: Malebranche thought the Fall changed the mind's relation to the body from partnership to dependence. This paper reconstructs what that feels like on his account - the body issuing demands the mind feels bound to meet - and argues he took those bodily obligations to be genuine, not illusions.
10.1093/arisoc/aoag023: If only today's voters with today's opinions should have a say, democracy looks doomed to short-termism and can never finish anything. Not so, the author argues: a democracy can treat past commitments as a strong default without betraying the principle that only the current public rules.
10.1086/739644: Constitutivists say the rules binding you come from what it is to be a rational agent at all. The trouble is that this forces them to find standards built into agency as such. This paper proposes a pluralist version: there are different kinds of rational agency, each with its own standards, which keeps the theory's advantages while allowing that some minimal agents are governed by no norms whatsoever.
10.1086/738316: What makes something a moral duty rather than merely a good idea? The proposal here: you are required to do something when your reasons to do it are also reasons for everyone else to expect it of you. That ties obligation to both private deliberation and the social emotions, and explains why going beyond duty is possible and why duty feels like a command.
10.1086/738309: Arguments against markets in kidneys, sex or surrogacy often say the transaction expresses something ugly, whatever its consequences. The paper sets out a dilemma: on either standard sense of 'meaning' the argument fails. A third, performative sense is a genuinely promising account of expressive reasoning in ethics - but it still won't support the case against commodification.
10.1086/738318: Does one theory of well-being cover humans, animals, and anything else whose life can go well or badly? Eden Lin argued yes; this paper argues no, objecting to his case and asking along the way what makes something a basic good for a given kind of creature.
10.1086/741046: Slack is having more than you strictly need: spare time, spare money, spare room, people who will cover for you. It lets you absorb shocks, take risks and fail without disaster, and it benefits the people around you too. The article argues slack is a distinct good that theories of freedom miss, and that pressure to optimise is steadily eroding it.
10.3998/phimp.4330: What makes two things one thing rather than two? The proposal here is modal: a=b holds because the two could not possibly have differed, and a is distinct from b because they could have. The author argues this is simpler and more intuitive than the alternatives, and preserves Leibniz's insight without expensive metaphysical commitments.
10.3998/phimp.6308: Saying 'this is indescribable' seems to do the very thing it denies is possible. The usual response is to explain how such sentences can be true. This paper takes the opposite route: they are always false - and shows that this does not make ineffability itself incoherent.
10.3998/phimp.7396: Jizang, a sixth-century Chinese Madhyamaka Buddhist, held that opposites make each other: there is no long without short, no self without other. The paper reconstructs this 'interdependence thesis', characterises the resulting metaphysics as a form of non-realism, and builds an argument that it is more plausible than it first sounds.
10.3998/phimp.7447: Almost everyone writing on discrimination assumes that to discriminate against someone is necessarily to put them at a disadvantage. Drawing on cases from the opioid epidemic - where patients were treated differently in ways that were not straightforwardly worse - this paper argues that assumption is wrong, which unsettles the standard way of distinguishing direct from indirect discrimination.
10.3998/phimp.7232: For many parents, raising a child is the project that gives their life its shape. The paper argues we owe each other non-interference with such projects, and that violence against children wrongs their parents by wrecking one - a wrong that falls disproportionately on mothers, and that has consequences for how we think about self-defence, punishment and war.
10.1353/hph.2025.a971096: Plato's word for the highest intellectual virtue was sophia, and scholars usually read it as knowing the Forms. This paper disagrees: wisdom in the Republic is the practical ability to judge well, by the Forms' standard, about what is best for the whole city or the whole soul - which changes how we read his quarrel with Protagoras and what he thought human beings can know.
10.1353/hph.2025.a971100: Schopenhauer is one of the very few philosophers to take malice seriously as a subject in its own right - the pleasure some people take in others' suffering. The paper reconstructs his account, which explains malice by the malicious person's own inner suffering, and works through the puzzles that account generates.
10.1353/hph.2025.a971183: The standard story is that Kant thought space was just relations between things until 1768, when thinking about left and right hands - mirror images that cannot be superimposed - abruptly changed his mind. This paper argues the story is wrong about both the timing and the reasons.
10.1353/hph.2026.a979223: Kant is usually read as claiming that things in themselves are not in space or time, which invites the objection that he never ruled out their being spatial anyway. The author reinterprets the claim: space is not a necessary condition on things as a kind. Read that way, the famous objection never gets started.
10.1353/hph.2026.a994284: Aristotle's treatment of friendship in the Eudemian Ethics is usually taken as proof that he is arguing dialectically, from common opinion. The paper argues he is doing something else: aiming at the truth about friendship, using both common and uncommon evidence, and preserving what is right in existing beliefs rather than merely reasoning from them.
10.5840/jphil202612312: Neo-logicists want to define number using Hume's Principle - two collections have the same number when they can be paired off exactly. The snag is that this principle adds mathematical content to pure logic, which a definition shouldn't. The author argues existing replies fail and proposes a version built on a two-sorted variant that genuinely is conservative, if you read conservativeness the right way.
10.5840/jphil2026123320: Grim Reaper puzzles - infinitely many assassins each set to act slightly earlier than the last - have been used to argue that time must be discrete and the past finite. The authors build a new version that needs only finitely many reapers, and use it to argue that the principles those finitist arguments rely on prove too much.
10.5840/jphil2026123322: The fewer Vermeers there are, the stronger our reason to protect each one. Bradford explained this with a notion of irreplaceable value. The authors offer a rival explanation grounded in the value of variety - a world containing more kinds of good thing is better - and argue it accounts for the pattern more economically.
10.5840/jphil20264117: How do you measure whether a set of beliefs hangs together? Existing proposals are built on two principles that look obviously right. The authors reject both, offer a probabilistic measure that honours the spirit of each without satisfying either, and show it does better at tracking truth - which, they argue, is the whole point of caring about coherence.
10.5840/jphil202642019: In a 1945 referee report, Alonzo Church sketched an argument that if every truth can be known, then every truth is already known - which would refute verificationism. The paper retells that history in Church's own logic, argues the classic arguments are not decisive, and then supplies new ones that are.
10.1093/mind/fzaf078: Marx dismissed equality as a bourgeois ideal, yet the best-known socialist critique of Rawls - G. A. Cohen's - rests entirely on an egalitarian principle, and Rawls's defenders have largely answered it. The author's diagnosis is that Cohen aimed at the right target with the wrong value, and builds an alternative around 'From each according to their abilities, to each according to their needs': an ideal of caring solidarity drawn from socialist, Christian and feminist traditions.
10.1093/mind/fzaf007: Schopenhauer's reputation as a hater of humanity is deserved but misleading - he objected to being called a misanthrope. Recent work separates a negative verdict on humankind from hatred of it, and the paper shows Schopenhauer offered two ways to hold the verdict without the hatred: substitute contempt, or revise the verdict itself.
10.1093/mind/fzaf023: Philosophers agree that the mind represents movement in some way that isn't language-like, but nobody has said what that representation is like. Drawing on neuroscience models of how the eye plans a saccade, the author argues some motor representations are literally map-shaped.
10.1093/mind/fzaf028: Virtue epistemology grades beliefs as skilful or clumsy. This paper extends the same treatment to questions: as truth is to answers, soundness - a question's admitting a true direct answer - is to questions. That yields standards for asking competently and aptly, and explains how asking well sets up answering well.
10.1093/mind/fzag037: Why does addiction sometimes excuse bad behaviour? Rather than asking what addiction is, the author asks what excuses do: they block inferences we would otherwise reasonably draw from someone's wrongdoing, helping us judge people as they actually deserve. The answer for addiction then falls out of that account.
10.1111/nous.70055: Reasoning is something you do, not something that happens to you. The argument is that reasoning is thinking shaped by what you already know - bias in a non-pejorative sense - because otherwise nothing would settle which of many available inferences to make. Empirical work on how beliefs steer attention supports the picture, and knowing how to reason turns out to be the structure that puts knowledge to work.
10.1111/nous.70038: Inquiring into a question means trying to answer it - so what counts as having answered? The puzzle is that judging something that happens to settle the question isn't enough; the judgement has to connect to the question in the right way, and nobody has said what that connection is. The paper names this the problem of answering and shows why it is hard.
10.1111/nous.70024: If the sets exist necessarily and are exactly as they are, why is that all of them - why no more? That question is the main argument for thinking the set hierarchy is always extendable. The author distinguishes three versions of that extendability view and argues the objection motivates none of them.
10.1111/nous.70033: Do you persist through time by being wholly present at each moment, or by having different temporal parts? McCall and Lowe claimed the two theories are equivalent, so there is no fact of the matter. Using a precise notion of equivalence borrowed from the philosophy of science, the author shows in exactly what sense they were right.
10.1111/nous.70035: Conversations come in kinds: sharing information or making decisions, committing or brainstorming, sticking to facts or playing pretend, cooperating or competing. The authors argue these genres are types of shared plan, and that speakers are under rational pressure to fit their plan - which gives listeners a powerful non-linguistic clue to what a speaker is doing.
10.1215/00318108-11964758: Almost everyone assumes a set of attitudes is coherent as long as it isn't incoherent. The paper argues that misses something: it cannot distinguish beliefs that positively support each other from beliefs that are merely unrelated. An alternative account built on support rather than the absence of conflict is proposed instead.
10.1215/00318108-11964820: Can two lives, or two outcomes, be genuinely incomparable - neither better, worse, nor equal? This paper says no, or much less often than people think. It uses two mild principles: one lottery beats another only if some outcome of the first beats some outcome of the second, and a lottery that gives some people better prospects and nobody worse ones is better.
10.1215/00318108-12453671: Could 2+2 have been 5? The paper takes the question seriously inside higher-order modal logic and finds surprising links to other questions in metaphysics. Its key move is to separate contingency about whether particular abstract objects are arranged a certain way from a deeper contingency about what holds of any objects so arranged.
10.1215/00318108-12240672: Consent theory says a government is legitimate only if the governed have agreed to it. Hume's objection - almost nobody has agreed - has marginalised the view, but consent theorists can shrug and accept anarchism. This article attacks the foundation instead: on almost any plausible account of why individual autonomy matters, autonomy does not in fact support consent theory.
10.1215/00318108-12323232: Sometimes another person's wrongdoing leaves you with a genuine duty - and discharging it makes you the instrument of the original wrong, or harms the very people you must help. You are compromised whether you act or not. The article argues such 'objectionable obligations' are perfectly coherent and are a useful tool for understanding subordination and exploitation.
10.1007/s11098-026-02532-y: If you have made the same journey a hundred times you can remember it without remembering any particular trip. The author argues this general kind of memory is not a degraded version of episodic memory but a case of representing an event whose time is genuinely indeterminate - an account that keeps the memory about the past, about particulars, and directly available.
10.1007/s11098-025-02409-6: If we ever build AI systems that matter morally for their own sake, we will need to know how to count them: is a model running on a thousand servers one patient or a thousand? The paper sets out four moral risks that follow from getting this wrong and explains why existing theories of personal identity do not help.
10.1007/s11098-026-02487-0: Philosophers prize theories that posit few things and few basic concepts, but these two kinds of economy have never been comparable. The author argues both reduce to one deeper demand - avoid brute, unexplained facts - which finally lets them be weighed against each other, with consequences for the debate about laws of nature.
10.1007/s11098-026-02479-0: Large language models are usually judged as failed models of the human mind. The author argues that is the wrong benchmark: linguistics also studies language as a public, social object, and as models of that, LLMs are genuinely informative. Recent interpretability work supplies what is needed to say what kind of model they are.
10.1007/s11098-025-02389-7: Experiments keep finding that people call a statement true if it was reasonable from the speaker's point of view, even when it is false - which conflicts with the philosophers' view that truth is correspondence to fact. The authors show the effect depends on the wording: ask 'Is it true that P?' and people apply correspondence; ask 'Is her answer true?' and they shift to the speaker's perspective.
10.1007/s11098-025-02433-6: Victims of grave injustice may be owed epistemic reparations - being believed, being known, having their account of what happened enter the record. The author applies this to disability, showing both how disabled people are wronged as knowers and how the concept of disability is itself used to discredit others, and argues progress is blocked while intellectual disability stays absent from social epistemology.
10.1007/s11098-026-02481-6: Hlobil and Brandom explain what follows from what using two speech acts, assertion and denial. Using cases involving 'might' and 'must', the author argues two are not enough - the account gets the wrong results about which claims are incompatible - and that moving to a richer set of acts fixes it.
10.1007/s11098-026-02501-5: Each of your beliefs may be justified while the conjunction of all of them is not - which is why many reject the idea that justification carries across 'and'. The authors argue that any decent account of understanding requires accepting that it does carry across, and draw out what follows.
10.1111/phpr.70122: Determinism sounds simple - the past fixes the future - but the many precise definitions on offer disagree and none delivers a clear verdict on actual physical theories. The authors argue for returning to a formal approach in which determinism is a property of theories rather than an elusive metaphysical doctrine, and show which formal criteria actually do the work.
10.1111/phpr.70125: Some philosophers argue on linguistic grounds that 'rational' and 'good' work like 'flat' or 'empty': strictly speaking only the perfect case counts. The author defends a middle position - these words carry demanding standards without requiring the maximum - which leaves room for infinite scales of value and lets talk of going beyond duty be literally true.
10.1111/phpr.70068: What is it to think 'people should exercise' - a general normative thought about no one in particular? The author argues it is neither an intention nor an evaluative belief but a settled disposition of the will, which then generates specific intentions and specific evaluations as circumstances call for them.
10.1111/phpr.70075: We normally think respect is owed to people because they can reason about what to do. The author argues the capacity to reason about what is true has the same structure, and so grounds a distinctively epistemic form of respect - which means you owe people belief in what they tell you unless you have some independent reason for doubt.
10.1111/phpr.70081: Standard consequentialism tells you to bring about the best outcome, including outcomes you cannot actually bring about - violating the rule that 'ought' implies 'can'. The author rejects two familiar repairs and defends a third, holism, which preserves both that rule and a workable account of what obligations are.
10.1093/pq/pqaf109: Suspending judgement comes in more than one flavour. Two are familiar: the evidence is evenly balanced, or there is no evidence either way. The authors argue for a third - aporetic suspension, the state of being genuinely stuck - which differs in what triggers it, what it makes you do, and how it feels.
10.1093/pq/pqaf098: Sometimes you want to know a fact; sometimes you want to make sense of something. The author argues these are different activities: inquiry aimed at knowledge ends by representing facts that were already there, while inquiry aimed at understanding builds a frame that organises information - which is why it is open-ended in a way knowledge-seeking is not.
10.1093/pq/pqaf102: Why should being able to feel confer moral status? Two standard answers are that consciousness is valuable to its bearer, and that it makes well-being possible. The author rejects both and argues sentience matters because it confers a level of welfare - not merely the capacity for one.
10.1093/pq/pqag004: Theories that judge actions by rules face a problem: they assess a rule by what would happen if lots of people followed it, which sometimes gives the wrong answer about what you should do now. This paper argues contractualism has the resources to keep the benefits - a principled way of making exceptions, and the independent importance of moral principles - without the awkward verdicts.
10.1093/pq/pqag015: We say things go well or badly for companies and countries. Can a group really have well-being, given that groups aren't conscious? The author argues the consciousness requirement as usually stated is both under-motivated and refuted by counterexample, and proposes a weaker version that lets groups have well-being while keeping the link between welfare and experience.
10.1007/s11229-026-05549-2: Human thinking looks like both a similarity-matcher and a probability calculator, and nobody has explained how the two fit together. This paper asks whether the conceptual-spaces account of concepts can slot into predictive processing, the leading Bayesian theory of the brain, and identifies concrete mechanisms - priors from region size, distance to a prototype - by which they could interlock.
10.1007/s11229-026-05698-4: We apologise for moral wrongs. The authors argue we also apologise for epistemic ones - for not believing someone, for asserting carelessly - and that these apologies do real work: repairing epistemic trust and epistemic relationships. The upshot is that moral and epistemic responsibility have the same conversational shape.
10.1007/s11229-026-05755-y: Should you trust a chatbot as a source of information? Applying the epistemology of trust, the author argues no - not because it is often wrong, but because it is unsafe: it could easily have told you something false in circumstances just like the actual ones. On that reading, believing what generative AI tells you is not a route to knowledge.
10.1007/s11229-025-05220-2: Feminist philosophy of logic asks whether formal systems can carry social bias. This paper connects queer feminist theory to paraconsistent logics - systems that tolerate contradictions among their theorems - arguing each has something the other needs: a real-world motivation for the logics, and a formal footing for a field that has been wary of formalism.
10.1007/s11229-025-05280-4: The authors ran experiments on how ordinary people, not doctors or philosophers, use 'healthy' and 'diseased'. The two turn out not to be opposites: people will call someone healthy who also has a disease. And whether something counts as a disease turns on facts about dysfunction rather than on whether it is bad for you.
10.1007/s11229-026-05454-8: Does machine learning in science smuggle in the assumptions of the field it is applied to? By comparing ML models with phenomenological models in physics, the authors argue model-building is largely indifferent to domain theory - it is 'infected' rather than laden - which matters for whether a model trained in one discipline can be moved to another.
10.1007/s11229-025-05345-4: A theory is categorical when all its models look alike. The authors reconstruct a categoricity proof for real analysis that Hilbert sketched in a 1905 lecture course, set it beside Dedekind's better-known 1888 result for arithmetic and Hilbert's own remarks on geometry, and ask why he wanted such arguments in the foundations of mathematics.
10.1007/s11229-025-05320-z: Sentence meanings and propositions never quite line up: many sentences say the same thing, and one sentence says different things in different contexts. The author proposes treating sentence meaning as a constraint on what can be said rather than a thing that is said, motivated especially by copredication - as in 'the book was heavy and hard to follow', where one word picks out an object and a content at once.
